title: ABA Required Disclosures — Employment Outcomes (Standard 509 / Employment Questionnaire), Classes of 2019-2025: dataset documentation and computed national series
pub: American Bar Association, Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar — Employment Questionnaire / Required Disclosures (abarequireddisclosures.org)
author: ABA Section of Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar

dom.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction

st.t: Graduate hiring: Strong outcomes mask entry contraction
st.an: The source materially strengthens the synthesis with a national ABA series showing that employed graduates and full-time, long-term bar-required employment fell from their 2024 peaks in 2025 while remaining above 2019 levels. It also reinforces the synthesis’s measurement cautions by distinguishing job measures and noting changes in the number of reporting schools, but it offers no causal account of the contraction or evidence about AI displacement.
qs: Firm-size rows count graduates employed in law firms of that size (all durations).

kp.k: National series aggregates school-level graduate counts
kp.d: The document presents a computed national series for the Classes of 2019–2025, created by summing per-school compilation spreadsheets and captured on August 29, 2026. All reported figures are graduate counts, not rates; FTLT means full-time, long-term employment.
qs: Computed national aggregate series (sums over per-school compilation spreadsheets; captured 2026-08-29)
All figures are counts of graduates. "FTLT" = full-time long-term.

kp.k: Outcomes are measured about ten months after graduation
kp.d: The ABA requires covered law schools to report each graduating class’s employment status approximately ten months after graduation. The series therefore measures an early-career outcome at a defined observation point, rather than graduates’ immediate placement or longer-term careers.
qs: Each spring, typically at the end of March or early April, all law schools enrolling students and approved or provisionally approved by the Council to offer the J.D. degree are required to report the employment outcomes of their graduates, reflecting their employment status approximately 10 months after graduation.

kp.k: Graduate and employment counts peaked in 2024
kp.d: Total graduates increased from 33,953 in 2019 to 38,936 in 2024 before falling to 36,208 in 2025. Total employed graduates followed a similar pattern, rising from 30,230 in 2019 to 36,015 in 2024 and then declining to 33,304 in 2025.

kp.k: Bar-required full-time long-term employment expanded overall
kp.d: Bar-admission-required FTLT employment rose from 24,475 graduates in 2019 to 29,951 in 2025, after reaching 31,696 in 2024. Total bar-required employment similarly increased from 25,044 to 30,213 over the full period, with a 2024 high of 32,024.
JD-advantage employment reached 3,718 graduates in 2021 and then declined each year, reaching 2,202 in 2025. The dataset records this shift but provides no causal explanation or connection to AI.

Employment at firms with 501 or more lawyers increased from 4,996 graduates in 2019 to 6,612 in 2025, with a peak of 7,145 in 2024. By comparison, placements at firms with 1–10 lawyers were 5,241 in 2019 and 5,405 in 2025, fluctuating within a narrower range.

kp.k: Unemployment peaked for the Class of 2020
kp.d: The number of unemployed graduates seeking work rose from 2,183 in 2019 to 2,855 in 2020, then fell to between 1,768 and 1,917 in each class from 2021 through 2025. The series reports counts and does not attribute the 2020 increase or subsequent decline to any cause.

kp.k: Sector outcomes shifted away from business and industry
kp.d: Business-and-industry employment declined from 3,485 graduates in 2019 to 2,294 in 2025. Government and public-interest employment were higher in 2025 than in 2019, although both peaked in 2024 and declined in 2025: government moved from 3,897 to 4,044, while public interest moved from 2,297 to 2,966.

kp.k: Firm-size figures include all employment durations
kp.d: The law-firm-size rows are not limited to full-time, long-term positions; they count graduates employed in firms of each size across all durations. They therefore should not be treated as directly equivalent to the separate bar-required FTLT measure.
qs: Firm-size rows count graduates employed in law firms of that size (all durations).

kp.k: Changing school counts qualify year-to-year comparisons
kp.d: The number of reporting schools declined from 198 in 2019 to 194 in 2024 before increasing to 195 in 2025. The documentation also states that column-name changes across reporting cycles were reconciled, both of which are relevant qualifications when comparing raw national counts over time.
qs: Column-name changes across cycles are reconciled as described in the note.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no concrete claims or predictions about AI.
pts.d: The document presents national law-graduate employment counts and ABA reporting documentation. It neither mentions AI nor attributes employment outcomes or changes in hiring to AI. Its descriptive employment series should not be recast as an AI-displacement or AI-augmentation claim.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Employment data are supplied, but not as evidence for an AI-related claim.
pts.d: The national series is described as sums over per-school compilation spreadsheets. It covers graduate employment statuses and employer categories, including firm-size bands. No AI adoption measures, AI exposure measures, or analysis connecting AI to these outcomes are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The data cover graduating classes of 2019–2025; no AI-related timeframe is stated.
pts.d: The reporting documentation describes employment snapshots approximately 10 months after graduation, rather than longitudinal career outcomes. These dates establish the scope of the dataset, not a timeline for AI effects.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: Recent J.D. graduates are the measured population, but no group is identified as affected by AI.
pts.d: The series distinguishes employment in law firms by size, business and industry, government, public interest, clerkships, and education. These are reporting categories; the document does not claim AI-driven effects on graduates, employers, clients, or the public.
